# Conclusion

This study asked whether adding freeze-frame features to an xG model improves its predictions compared with a model that only uses distance, angle, body part, assist type and play pattern. The answer is yes, but the improvement is modest. Adding the standard spatial features lowered the XGBoost Brier score from 0.0776 to 0.0737, and the full feature set reached 0.0728, which is about 6% better than the baseline, or roughly five percentage points of Brier skill. The improvement appeared for both XGBoost and logistic regression, with and without the event-context features, and both inside and outside the penalty box, so it was consistent even though it was small.

The three hypotheses were supported to different degrees. Hypothesis 1 was supported, because spatial features improved predictions across all the probability measures. Hypothesis 2 was not supported in practice, because the extended spatial features improved the Brier score by only 0.2%, even though the difference was statistically detectable. Hypothesis 3 was supported, because the improvement was larger inside the box (5.5% compared with 2.3%). In answer to the research questions, a standard xG model (M1) performs reasonably well but trails StatsBomb's xG by about 5% in Brier score (Question 1), the most important spatial features were the shooter-to-goalkeeper distance (`DistSGK`) and `goal_blocked` (Question 2), and the improvement from spatial features was larger close to goal (Question 3).

Three broader points come out of the results. Firstly, which features are used matters more than which algorithm: XGBoost was never more than 1.3% better than logistic regression, and a logistic regression with good features beat an XGBoost model with fewer. Secondly, a small, well-chosen set of freeze-frame features gives nearly all the benefit, so a large amount of additional feature engineering is hard to justify. Thirdly, the best models were competitive with StatsBomb's own xG on probability and ranking measures, using only open data, which suggests that analysts can build useful xG models of their own.

These conclusions apply to open-play shots in men's football, taken from a sample dominated by one season, and the limitations in Section 6.3 should be kept in mind, particularly the varying completeness of freeze frames. Even so, the study shows that knowing where the defenders and goalkeeper are standing gives a reliable, if small, improvement to how well we can judge the quality of a shot.
